name: ADUM1201ARZ-RL7
title: Dual-channel digital isolators, ADuM1200 and ADuM1201
summary: Two-channel digital isolators that pass logic signals across a 2500 V rms barrier using on-chip transformers (iCoupler) in place of LEDs and photodiodes. The ADuM1200 carries both channels from side 1 to side 2; the ADuM1201 carries one each way. Each side runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V on its own supply, so the part also shifts between 3 V and 5 V logic. Speed grades run to 1, 10 or 25 Mbps, in an 8-lead narrow SOIC, with W automotive grades rated to 125 °C.
key_figures: 2.7 V to 5.5 V (W grades 3.0 V to 5.5 V)
1.1 mA per channel max, DC to 2 Mbps

Minimum pulse width and maximum data rate are the limits within which the listed pulse width distortion holds.
tPHL runs from the 50% point of the falling input edge to the 50% point of the falling output edge; tPLH is the same between rising edges.
tPSK is the largest spread in tPHL or tPLH between separate units held at one temperature, supply voltage and load inside the recommended operating conditions.

Codirectional matching is the largest propagation delay difference between two channels whose inputs are on one side of the barrier; opposing directional matching is the same for channels whose inputs are on opposite sides.

Dynamic supply current is the added supply current for each 1 Mbps rise in data rate.

operation.text: The ADuM1200 has two channels running from side 1 (VDD1, GND1) to side 2 (VDD2, GND2). The ADuM1201 has channel A running from side 2 to side 1 and channel B from side 1 to side 2. Each side has its own supply and ground.

Every rising or falling input edge sends a pulse of about 1 ns across the transformer to a bistable decoder, which it sets or resets. When the input has not changed for more than about 1 µs, refresh pulses carrying the present input level are sent so the output stays correct at DC. If the decoder sees no pulses for more than about 5 µs, a watchdog takes the input side to be unpowered or faulty and drives the output to its default level given in the truth tables.

With the input-side supply off, the ADuM1200 outputs and the ADuM1201's side 2 output go high; the ADuM1201's side 1 output, whose own supply is off, is indeterminate. With the output-side supply off, that side's outputs are indeterminate. Outputs follow the inputs again within 1 µs of the missing supply coming back.

The logic pins need no external parts. A bypass capacitor of 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF belongs on each supply, at the input and at the output side. The lead length from both ends of the capacitor to the supply pin must total no more than 20 mm. Analog Devices application note AN-1109 covers board layout.

Propagation delay is the input-to-output delay of one edge, measured between 50% points; the delay to a low output and to a high output can differ. Pulse width distortion is the largest difference between those two delays and shows how faithfully pulse timing comes through. The largest delay difference between channels of one part is its channel-to-channel matching; between separate parts under the same conditions it is the propagation delay skew.

An external field disturbs the part only if it induces enough voltage in a receiving coil to set or reset the decoder falsely. At 3 V, the weakest case, the transformer delivers pulses above 1.0 V and the decoder threshold is about 0.5 V. The allowable field curve holds the induced voltage to half of that 0.5 V margin: at 1 MHz the limit is 0.2 kgauss, which induces 0.25 V. If such a field coincides with a transmitted pulse of the worst polarity, the pulse drops from above 1.0 V to 0.75 V, still over the threshold. As a current, at 1 MHz it takes 0.5 kA passing 5 mm from the part to upset it. Loops of board trace near strong high-frequency fields can pick up enough voltage to trip circuits that follow the isolator, so such traces need care in layout.

Each channel's supply current depends on the supply voltage, its data rate and its output load. Below half the refresh rate a channel draws its quiescent current; above it, current rises with data rate by the dynamic figure, and on the output side also with load capacitance and supply voltage. The total from VDD1 or VDD2 is the sum of the input and output channel currents on that side.

Insulation wears out under long voltage stress, at a rate set by the waveform across the barrier. Analog Devices sets working voltages from accelerated life tests at raised voltage, beyond the agency testing. Bipolar AC is the hardest case, and its 50-year lifetime gives the 565 V peak figure. Unipolar AC, a waveform that varies between 0 V and a limit of either sign without crossing 0 V, and DC stress the insulation much less, so the higher approved working voltages hold for 50 years with them. Any waveform that is neither unipolar AC nor DC is treated as bipolar AC and limited to 565 V peak. The approved working voltage often exceeds the 50-year voltage, and running at it can shorten insulation life in some cases.

The ADuM1200W and ADuM1201W are made under controlled manufacturing for automotive use and are qualified to 125 °C. Their specifications can differ from the commercial grades; the 125 °C tables apply to them. Only the W models are for automotive applications.
